title: Genomics with Ngan
text:
orcid = '0000-0000-0000-0000' # Fill your orcid here


import requests

We use the /works api to list all works related to the orcid. This gives a summary of all works, so citation information is not included. We collect the put-code of all works to retrieve the citation information later.

response = requests.get('https://pub.orcid.org/v3.0/{}/works'.format(orcid),
                        headers={"Accept": "application/orcid+json" })
record = response.json()


put_codes = []
for work in record['group']:
    put_code = work['work-summary'][0]['put-code']
    put_codes.append(put_code)
put_code = put_codes[0]

We use the /<orcid>/work/<put-code> endpoint to retrieve the citation information for each record.

citations = []
for put_code in put_codes:
    response = requests.get('https://pub.orcid.org/v3.0/{}/work/{}'.format(orcid, put_code),
                            headers={"Accept": "application/orcid+json" })
    work = response.json()
    if work['citation'] is not None:
        citations.append(work['citation']['citation-value'])


with open('output.bib', 'w') as bibfile:
    for citation in citations:
        bibfile.write(citation)
        bibfile.write('\n')

title: Welcome to Genomics with Ngan
text: This blog is my attempt to write publicly about the things I spend my days thinking about: population genetics, statistical genomics, and the challenge of understanding human genetic diversity in all its complexity.

title: Welcome to Genomics with Ngan
text:
What you’ll find here
A few times a month I plan to post:

Methods tutorials — walkthroughs of tools like PLINK, ADMIXTURE, VCFtools, and SMC++ with real code and real output. The kind of post I wish had existed when I was learning.
Paper commentary — my read on new preprints and publications in the pop-gen space. What’s interesting, what’s novel, what I’m skeptical about.
Analysis walkthroughs — worked examples using R, usually including the actual code blocks so you can follow along or adapt them to your own data.
Opinion pieces — occasional longer-form thoughts on where the field is heading, equity in genomics research, and what it means to do population genetics responsibly with underrepresented groups.

title: Welcome to Genomics with Ngan
text:
Who this is for
Broadly: scientists and students who are curious about population genetics but aren’t necessarily specialists. I’ll assume you’re comfortable with basic genetics and statistics, but I’ll try to explain the population-genetics-specific concepts rather than assuming everyone has read Hartl & Clark cover to cover.

title: Welcome to Genomics with Ngan
text:
A note on the research
My work focuses mainly on Indigenous Australian and Southeast Asian populations — groups that are genomically understudied relative to their diversity and their disease burden. A lot of standard pop-gen methods were developed and validated on European-ancestry cohorts. Understanding where they work, where they break down, and how to do better is one of the central questions I keep coming back to.
More soon.

title: Jupyter notebook markdown generator
text:
Jupyter notebook markdown generator
These .ipynb files are Jupyter notebook files that convert a TSV containing structured data about talks (talks.tsv) or presentations (presentations.tsv) into individual markdown files that will be properly formatted for the academicpages template. The notebooks contain a lot of documentation about the process. The .py files are pure python that do the same things if they are executed in a terminal, they just don’t have pretty documentation.

title: Leaflet cluster map of talk locations
text:
Assuming you are working in a Linux or Windows Subsystem for Linux environment, you may need to install some dependencies. Assuming a clean installation, the following will be needed:
sudo apt install jupyter
sudo apt install python3-pip
pip install python-frontmatter getorg --upgrade
After which you can run this from the _talks/ directory, via:
 jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute talkmap.ipynb --output talkmap_out.ipynb
The _talks/ directory contains .md files of all your talks. This scrapes the location YAML field from each .md file, geolocates it with geopy/Nominatim, and uses the getorg library to output data, HTML, and Javascript for a standalone cluster map.

# Perform geolocation
for file in g:
    # Read the file
    data = frontmatter.load(file)
    data = data.to_dict()

    # Press on if the location is not present
    if 'location' not in data:
        continue

    # Prepare the description
    title = data['title'].strip()
    venue = data['venue'].strip()
    location = data['location'].strip()
    description = f"{title}<br />{venue}; {location}"

    # Geocode the location and report the status
    try:

        print(description, location_dict[description])
    except ValueError as ex:
        print(f"Error: geocode failed on input {location} with message {ex}")
    except GeocoderTimedOut as ex:
        print(f"Error: geocode timed out on input {location} with message {ex}")
    except Exception as ex:
        print(f"An unhandled exception occurred while processing input {location} with message {ex}")

    Kim Ngan Tran
    Computational population geneticist · Brisbane, Australia

    I work at the intersection of population genetics, statistical genomics, and human health — with a particular focus on understanding how genetic diversity shapes disease risk across populations that have historically been underrepresented in genomic research.

    My research uses large-scale genomic data to study population structure, runs of homozygosity, autozygosity, and complex trait architecture in Indigenous Australian and Southeast Asian populations. I'm interested in both the methods and the biology: how do we build tools that work equitably across diverse human populations, and what do those populations tell us about the evolutionary and demographic forces that shaped human genetic variation?

    This blog is where I think out loud about population genetics — methods tutorials, paper commentary, analysis walkthroughs, and occasional opinion pieces. The intended audience is curious scientists and students who want to understand what the field is actually doing.

    Research interests
    
      Population structure
      Autozygosity & ROH
      GWAS in diverse populations
